Four Circles In Triangle

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: a triangle holds one big circle and three smaller circles, with three lines joining the places where they touch.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus one of them and press the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the lines, touch points and names, and press Reset triangle to start over.
Look for the math

Move a corner and every circle moves too. Yet the three lines drawn through the touching points keep meeting at a single spot. Here is why that is not an accident.

Four circles, one pattern

First comes the incircle: it touches all three sides of the triangle. Each small circle in a corner is just a shrunken copy of that incircle, centred on the line from the corner to the incircle's centre. If the distance from corner A to the incenter is D and the big radius is r, the copy's radius is r × t with t = (D − r) / (D + r). Since D = r / sin(A/2), this is t = (1 − sin(A/2)) / (1 + sin(A/2)). The logic test checks all three circles this way in hundreds of triangles.

The two ends of each line

One end is where the incircle touches a side: the foot of the perpendicular from its centre. The other is where the incircle touches the small circle at the opposite corner. That point sits on the incircle, exactly r from its centre towards the corner. It is equally far around the circle from the two neighbouring side touch points, so it is the midpoint of the arc they cut off — the arc opposite that corner.

Why they concur

The three side touch points form the contact triangle. In that triangle, a line from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite arc is an angle bisector. The page's claim follows: the three lines meet at the incenter of the contact triangle. The logic test measured the third line's distance from the meeting point in 238 drawable triangles: always below 0.000001 board units, and the point matched that incenter.

Small applet quirks

The original stops drawing when the big radius is below half a unit, and its quadratic solver rejects very nearly straight triangles where the corner and the incenter are almost one radius apart. This page keeps both guards, so a nearly flat triangle can have no picture. The three checkboxes and Reset are modern conveniences; they never change the geometry. The theorem is attributed on the original page to Evelyn, Money-Coutts and Tyrrell, The Seven Circles Theorem and Other New Theorems (1974), and is a special case of the Seven Circles Theorem.

Try moving one corner until the triangle is almost flat. Which happens first: the circles becoming tiny, or the picture disappearing altogether?
